concepts.name: Purpose and Rationale for Base Year Revision
key_dimensions: Why base years become outdated: structural shifts in economy, emergence of new sectors, changing consumption patterns
Role of base year in eliminating price distortions and reflecting real economic activity
International best practice: UN System of National Accounts (SNA) recommendation to revise every 5-10 years
UPSC trap: Distinguishing between 'base year revision' and 'rebasing' vs 'methodological overhaul' — the 2011-12 revision involved BOTH

concepts.name: Historical Sequence of Base Year Revisions in India
key_dimensions: Agency responsible: Central Statistics Office (CSO), now NSO under MoSPI
Frequency analysis: Gap between revisions and its economic implications
UPSC trap: Confusing the current base year (2011-12) with the previous one (2004-05); questions often ask which revision introduced GVA prominently

concepts.name: 2011-12 Base Year Revision: Key Methodological Changes
key_dimensions: Shift from GDP at Factor Cost to Gross Value Added (GVA) at Basic Prices as the primary measure
Adoption of SNA 2008 framework replacing SNA 1993
New data sources: MCA21 database for corporate sector, expanded NSSO surveys
UPSC trap: GVA at Basic Prices ≠ GVA at Factor Cost — Basic Prices include production taxes/subsidies but exclude product taxes/subsidies

concepts.name: GDP vs GVA: Relationship Post-2011-12 Revision
key_dimensions: Formula: GDP = GVA at Basic Prices + Product Taxes – Product Subsidies
Why India shifted headline reporting to GVA: better sectoral analysis, isolates impact of tax-subsidy distortions
Difference between 'factor cost,' 'basic prices,' and 'market prices' — a classic UPSC confusion zone
Policy implication: A high product subsidy regime can make GDP significantly different from GVA, masking sectoral productivity

concepts.name: MCA21 Database Integration in National Accounts
key_dimensions: What MCA21 is: Ministry of Corporate Affairs' electronic registry of company filings
How its integration improved GDP estimates: coverage of ~5 lakh private companies vs earlier sample-based approach
Controversy: Initial estimates showed higher GDP growth partly due to better corporate coverage, not actual acceleration
UPSC trap: MCA21 improved the 'corporate sector' estimate — it does NOT cover unorganised/informal sector estimates

concepts.name: Treatment of Unorganised/Informal Sector in Revised Estimates
key_dimensions: Methodology: Enterprise surveys, NSSO surveys, and extrapolation using formal sector as proxy
Criticism post-2011-12: Overestimation of informal sector growth by benchmarking it to formal sector trends
Demonetisation debate: Whether GDP estimates captured informal sector contraction accurately
UPSC angle: Informal sector contributes ~45% of GDP but is hardest to measure — this is a recurring limitation question

concepts.name: Impact of Base Year Revision on GDP Growth Rate Estimates
key_dimensions: Backdating controversy: Revised series showed India's GDP growth higher than previously estimated for 2012-14
Comparison with IMF/World Bank estimates and the credibility debate
Statistical artifact vs real growth: How methodological changes can arithmetically alter growth figures
UPSC trap: Revised GDP numbers do NOT mean the economy actually grew faster — it reflects better measurement

concepts.name: Advance Estimates, Revised Estimates, and Final Estimates System
key_dimensions: First Advance Estimate (FAE): Released in January of the fiscal year — basis for Union Budget
Chain of revisions: 1st AE → 2nd AE → 1st RE → 2nd RE → Final Estimates (released ~2 years later)
Why large revisions occur: Incomplete data for agriculture, informal sector, and government expenditure
UPSC trap: The Union Budget is presented using First Advance Estimate GDP — not the final figure

concepts.name: Nominal GDP vs Real GDP in the Context of Base Year
key_dimensions: Definition distinction: Nominal GDP uses current prices; Real GDP deflates using base year prices
GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100 — different from CPI/WPI
Why base year choice affects Real GDP: An outdated base year with old price structures distorts volume estimates
UPSC trap: GDP deflator is a broader price index than CPI/WPI as it covers all goods and services produced

concepts.name: Chain-Base Method vs Fixed-Base Method
key_dimensions: Fixed-base: All years compared to single base year — simple but becomes less representative over time
Chain-base: Each year compared to previous year, then linked — more dynamic but complex
India's current approach: Fixed base (2011-12) with periodic revisions — NOT yet moved to chain-linking
UPSC angle: Advanced economies (US, UK) use chain-linking; India's shift to chain-base is a pending reform often cited in Economic Survey

concepts.name: Sectoral Reclassification in 2011-12 Revision
key_dimensions: New sector breakdown: Agriculture, Industry, Services with sub-categories aligned to NIC 2008
Financial services: FISIM (Financial Intermediation Services Indirectly Measured) now explicitly calculated
R&D expenditure reclassified: From intermediate consumption to capital formation (investment) — per SNA 2008
UPSC trap: Treating R&D as investment INCREASES GDP — this is a methodological change, not actual new investment

concepts.name: FISIM (Financial Intermediation Services Indirectly Measured)
key_dimensions: Definition: Imputed value of banking services for which no explicit fee is charged (spread between lending and deposit rates)
SNA 2008 mandates its inclusion — adds to service sector GDP
India began including FISIM in 2011-12 revision, inflating financial services contribution
UPSC trap: FISIM is NOT a direct tax or fee — it is an imputed/estimated value, making it a common conceptual confusion point

concepts.name: Treatment of Government Expenditure and Public Sector in National Accounts
key_dimensions: Government output measured at cost (since no market price): Sum of compensation + intermediate consumption + consumption of fixed capital
Defence expenditure: Revenue expenditure = intermediate consumption; Capital expenditure = Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF)
UPSC trap: Government services are NOT valued at market price — this leads to systematic undervaluation vs private sector
Post-revision improvement: Better use of CAG data and state finance accounts for government sector estimation

concepts.name: Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) and Its Revised Measurement
key_dimensions: GFCF as a proxy for investment: Includes machinery, construction, intellectual property (post-SNA 2008)
2011-12 change: Intellectual property products (software, R&D, mineral exploration) now included in GFCF
Private vs Public GFCF trends: Declining public investment, crowding-in vs crowding-out debate
UPSC trap: GFCF ≠ total investment — it excludes changes in inventories and valuables (gold/silver), which are separate components of capital formation

concepts.name: Institutional Framework: CSO, NSO, and MoSPI
key_dimensions: CSO (Central Statistics Office) merged with NSSO to form NSO under MoSPI in 2019
National Statistical Commission (NSC): Autonomous body to oversee statistical standards — its recommendations on base year revision
Back Series controversy: NSC's committee (Sudipto Mundle Committee) could not reconcile back series data — government released its own figures
UPSC trap: NSC is an advisory body, NOT a constitutional body — MoSPI retains final authority on GDP release

concepts.name: Back Series Controversy After 2011-12 Revision
key_dimensions: Problem: New methodology (SNA 2008, GVA framework) needed to be applied backwards to compare with old series
NSC-appointed Sudipto Mundle Committee submitted report but government released different figures in November 2018
Key dispute: Revised back series showed UPA-era growth lower and NDA-era growth higher — politicisation of statistics
UPSC angle: Highlights tension between statistical integrity and political optics — a governance and institutional credibility issue

concepts.name: Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) vs Market Exchange Rate in Cross-Country Comparisons
key_dimensions: PPP-based GDP: Adjusts for price level differences across countries — makes India's economy appear larger (3rd largest by PPP)
Market exchange rate GDP: Uses prevailing forex rate — India ranks 5th/6th
ICP (International Comparison Programme) under World Bank: Provides PPP conversion factors, updated periodically
UPSC trap: Base year for domestic GDP and base year for PPP comparison are DIFFERENT exercises — PPP is for international comparison, not domestic deflation

concepts.name: Per Capita Income Estimation and Its Limitations Post-Revision
key_dimensions: Formula: Per Capita NNI = NNI at Current Prices / Mid-year Population
Population data source: Census (decennial) with interpolation — creates estimation error between census years
Post-2011-12: Per capita income figures revised upward, but welfare implications questioned given inequality
UPSC trap: Per capita INCOME uses NNI (not GDP) at current prices — students often confuse GDP per capita with per capita NNI

concepts.name: National Income Aggregates: Conceptual Hierarchy and Traps
key_dimensions: Hierarchy: GDP → GNP (add Net Factor Income from Abroad) → NNP (deduct Depreciation) → National Income (NNI at Factor Cost)
Post-revision: NNI at Factor Cost = GVA at Basic Prices + NFIA – Net Production Taxes
Depreciation (Consumption of Fixed Capital): Estimated, not directly measured — a weak link in national accounts

UPSC trap: GNP > GDP if NFIA is positive (India historically has negative NFIA due to profit repatriation by MNCs exceeding remittance inflows — VERIFY each year as remittances now make NFIA positive)

concepts.name: Upcoming Base Year Revision to 2022-23: Anticipated Changes
key_dimensions: MoSPI announced revision to 2022-23 base year — expected to incorporate post-COVID structural shifts
New data sources anticipated: GST network data (GSTN), digital payment data, gig economy estimation
SNA 2025 (forthcoming): May influence methodology — treatment of data as capital asset under discussion
UPSC angle: GSTN integration expected to significantly improve informal sector estimation — a major limitation of 2011-12 revision that may be addressed
